newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese President Jiang Zemin leaves for Russia.
newsitem.headline: Chinese President Jiang Zemin leaves for Russia.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin left on Tuesday for a five-day visit to Russia aimed at building ties between two giants who view each other as key strategic partners in the next century.

Jiang was travelling with his wife, Wang Yeping, as well as Vice-Premier and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, Defence Minister Chi Haotian and his special assistant and top advisor Zeng Qinghong, the official Xinhua news agency said.
During his visit, Jiang is to hold talks with Russian President Boris Yeltsin and with him sign a political declaration outlining a joint vision of the future world order.

Jiang, Yeltsin and the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan will also sign a treaty on reducing armed forces along the former Soviet-Chinese border. Details of the treaty have not been made public.

Russia, deeply unhappy about NATO's plans to expand eastwards, is looking for new allies elsewhere. China, under heavy pressure from the West over alleged human rights violations, is among the most attractive candidates.
Moscow and Beijing have made clear they are poised to set an example for other countries on how to maintain security and build bilateral ties.

In Moscow, Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the bilateral political declaration, the first such document signed since Moscow and Beijing started to repair ties in the late 1980s after more than two decades of hostility, would speak out against any country playing the role of absolute leader.
He did not name any state but both Moscow and Beijing have been critical of Washington's domination of the post-Cold War world order.

Apart from political benefits, Moscow clearly hopes for better trade relations with Beijing that would bring greater access to the vast Chinese market and to markets in Southeast Asia and the Pacific Rim.
Itar-Tass news agency said two-way trade reached $6.9 billion in 1996, 25 percent higher than the previous year. The balance is lopsided in Russia's favour to the tune of around $3.5 billion.
Moscow officials have said that trade turnover could reach $8-10 billion in 1997 and $20 billion by the end of the century.
Russia hopes to boost arms sales to China from current levels of around $1 billion a year. Some estimates say this could be up to 30 percent of Moscow's overall arms exports.
The two countries have yet to finalise the demarcation of their long border, however.
The Kremlin has faced angry protests from influential leaders of its Far Eastern regions who say a new proposed borderline is unjust and insist that it be reviewed.
